title: FIFA Fires COO Kevin Lamour as Infantino Faces Growing Revolt
excerpt: FIFA dismissed its chief operating officer after he accused President Gianni Infantino of deception, as Norway demands his resignation and UEFA maintains its boycott threat.
body:
• FIFA fired Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour on August 17 after he publicly accused President Gianni Infantino of "deception" over a controversial World Cup stake-sale plan.
  • Norway's football federation president Lise Klaveness has called on Infantino to resign, saying "the trust is now gone" and there is "no way back."
  • UEFA has declared it no longer has confidence in Infantino and maintains its threat to boycott all FIFA competitions.
  • The crisis stems from Infantino's abandoned plan to create a $20 billion subsidiary and sell up to 20% of FIFA's tournament business to private investors.

FIFA confirmed on Monday that its Chief Operating Officer Kevin Lamour has been dismissed, weeks after the Frenchman publicly accused President Gianni Infantino of deceiving the organization's administration over a controversial plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

"FIFA can confirm that the working relationship between FIFA and Kevin Lamour as FIFA's Chief Operating Officer has ended on 17 August 2026," a FIFA spokesperson told Reuters. "FIFA thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future."

Lamour's Downfall

Described by Le Monde as FIFA's "number three," Lamour had served as COO since November 2024 and was once part of Infantino's inner circle during his 2016 presidential campaign. But on July 31, he broke ranks in spectacular fashion.

"This lie by omission over many months and this unilateral exercise of power are not trivial. They are indicative of a lack of trust, a lack of transparency, a lack of discernment, a lack of good governance. And a serious lack of respect."

— Kevin Lamour, former FIFA COO

Lamour told the Associated Press that FIFA staff had been "deceived" and called the proposal "the project of one person." He added: "If that means I lose my job, then so be it. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

His departure was announced by FIFA Secretary General Mattias Grafstrom in an email to staff and FIFA Council members. While FIFA characterized it as a mutual parting, both The Times and Sky News reported that Lamour was fired.

Growing Revolt Against Infantino

Lamour's exit came on the same day the Scottish Football Association declared it would not support Infantino's re-election bid. But the most significant blow arrived from Norway, where football federation president Lise Klaveness called for Infantino's immediate resignation.

"We decided that there is no trust in Infantino now," Klaveness told The Guardian. "We have been worried consistently and there has been one more step in worrying direction every year. The trust is now gone for us, there is no way back for Infantino."

UEFA, European football's governing body, has formally declared it no longer has confidence in the FIFA president and maintains its threat to boycott all FIFA competitions. The English Football Association has also withdrawn support for Infantino's re-election, set for March 2027.

The Crisis Behind the Chaos

The turmoil traces back to Infantino's proposal to create a subsidiary called the FIFA Forward Enterprise — a $20 billion entity that would run FIFA's tournaments, including the World Cup, with up to 20% sold to private investors. Three continental confederations rejected the plan outright, and it was withdrawn on August 1 after sustained backlash.

Lamour was not the first senior figure to break with Infantino. Carlos Cordeiro, a senior adviser and former U.S. Soccer president, resigned in protest on July 31, saying "I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup." Arsene Wenger, FIFA's chief of global football development, also distanced himself from the proposal.

UEFA Vice-President Laura McAllister said Lamour's sacking "seriously weakens FIFA's administration, whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA."

Infantino Still Has Backing

Despite the European revolt, Infantino retains significant support among FIFA's 211 member associations. The Confederation of African Football unanimously backed his leadership, while South America's CONMEBOL rejected any attempt to oust him outside a formal vote. Qatar, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Morocco — which will co-host the 2030 World Cup — have all declared loyalty.

An Extraordinary Congress could theoretically be convened if 43 or more member associations submit a formal written request. No clear challenger to Infantino has yet emerged for the March election, though the crisis has cast a deepening shadow over his bid for a fourth term.
